issues.legal_issue: The scope of an appeal is not confined to an initially limited notice when leave to appeal is subsequently granted.
material_facts: The initial notice was confined to whether the Collector had power to act under the law governing intestate estates in light of the legislation concerning administration of estates.
Leave to appeal was subsequently granted, and the State argued that the Court should address only the issue identified in the initial notice.
issues.conclusion: The initial limitation did not restrict the scope of the appeal after leave was granted; the Court could consider all contentions, guided by the advancement of substantial justice.
issues.legal_principle: The Court’s inherent powers under Order XLVII Rule 6 of the Supreme Court Rules, 1966, and its power to do complete justice under Article 142 are not limited by tentative observations or orders made when notice is issued. Whether to consider the full controversy after leave is granted is a matter of judicial discretion guided by substantial justice. The Court relied on Yomeshbhai Pranshankar Bhatt v State of Gujarat, State of Uttaranchal v Alok Sharma, and Indian Bank v Godhara Nagrik Cooperative Credit Society.

predicates.appeal_with_leave_granted: A court is hearing an appeal in which leave to appeal has been granted.
predicates.initial_notice_limited: The notice issued at the initial stage confined the matter to a limited issue.

issues.definition: When an appeal has proceeded from a limited initial notice to the grant of leave, its scope is not confined to that notice.

issues.legal_issue: An administrative officer cannot adjudicate disputed private title claims in order to determine that property has escheated to the government.
material_facts: The government claimed that property registered in the name of an individual had escheated because that individual had died without an heir.
A trust claimed an interest in the property based on its account of the acquisition, a will, a declaration by the registered owner, and its long management and occupation of the property.

The competing claims raised disputed questions about the source of the purchase funds, the validity and effect of documents, the identity and death of the registered owner, and the existence of heirs.
The Collector resolved those factual disputes and ordered that possession be taken, although the governing escheat provision supplied no procedure for adjudicating disputed questions of title.
issues.conclusion: The Collector acted in excess of jurisdiction by adjudicating the competing claims. The Collector’s order was set aside, without the Court determining whether the trust had valid title; disputed title matters must be pursued in a competent civil court.
issues.legal_principle: Section 29 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, provides for government devolution when an intestate leaves no qualified heir, and the government takes subject to the obligations and liabilities to which an heir would have been subject. Escheat requires a total absence of heirs, and the burden of establishing that absence rests heavily on the party asserting escheat; the Court relied on State of Punjab v Balwant Singh and State of Bihar v Radha Krishna Singh, which also emphasizes public notice before entertaining an escheat claim. A state authority cannot exercise adjudicatory powers over private civil disputes unless the law confers them; such title disputes fall within ordinary civil jurisdiction under Section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, unless excluded by law. The Administrators-General Act, 1963, including Sections 7 and 9–12, 14 and 20, provides for estate protection and administration through applications to, and adjudication by, the High Court; it does not confer judicial power on the Collector. The Court also relied on Rambir Das v Kalyan Das and Mahant Sital Das v Sant Ram concerning the devolution and regulation of religious endowments.

rule.if: administrative_escheat_proceeding and administrative_officer_decides_property_claim and competing_private_title_claims and disputed_facts_require_title_adjudication

predicates.administrative_escheat_proceeding: An administrative proceeding is used to determine whether property should pass to the government because an owner allegedly died without an heir.
predicates.administrative_officer_decides_property_: An administrative officer resolves who owns or is entitled to property.
predicates.competing_private_title_claims: A private person or entity asserts an interest in property contrary to the government’s claim.
predicates.disputed_facts_require_title_adjudicatio: The competing claims depend on contested facts that require adjudication of title or entitlement.

issues.definition: When an administrative officer determines an escheat claim despite competing private title claims that depend on disputed facts, the officer lacks jurisdiction to adjudicate title.

issues.legal_issue: A Collector’s power to take possession or evict an occupant under the land-transfer provision is available only when the statutory conditions for vesting following a void transfer are met.
material_facts: The State relied on a provision authorizing the Collector to take possession of property vested in the State under the preceding provision concerning transfers that are void by law.

The State’s claim in this matter was that the property had passed to it by escheat because the owner allegedly had no heir; the case did not involve property shown to have vested under the void-transfer provision.
issues.conclusion: The possession and eviction power was not available because the circumstances specified in the preceding void-transfer provision were not present.
issues.legal_principle: Section 167(2) of the Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, as applicable in the State, permits the Collector to take possession or evict an occupant only where property has vested in the State under Section 167(1), which concerns transfers void under Section 166. The Court held that Section 167(2) was not attracted in this case.

predicates.land_reform_possession_proceeding: A proceeding seeks to use an administrative power to take possession of property or evict an occupant under a land-transfer regime.
predicates.property_vested_following_void_transfer: The property vested in the government because it was the subject of a transfer declared void under the applicable law.

issues.definition: In a land-reform possession or eviction proceeding, the Collector cannot use the statutory possession or eviction power unless the property vested in the government following a void transfer.
